standard.title: Growing plants and animals
standard.description: explore how plants and animals are grown for food, clothing and shelter
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have explored how products are designed and produced to meet community needs (AC9TDE2K01). They understand that design decisions connect to purpose. They have not yet examined the origins of the materials used in products — specifically that plants and animals are deliberately grown and managed as sources for food, clothing and shelter.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explore how plants and animals are grown and used as sources for food, clothing and shelter, identifying specific plants and animals and the products derived from them.

nodes.label: Plants and animals as sources for products
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify which plants and animals provide food, materials for clothing, or materials for shelter
nodes.minimum_width: Sort at least three familiar items into plant-source or animal-source categories; name one plant and one animal used as a source for food, clothing or shelter
nodes.typical_width: Identify a range of plants and animals as sources across food, clothing and shelter categories; give examples of products derived from each source; explain the relationship between the plant or animal and the product
wider: Explore how First Nations Australians grow plants and animals for food — for example the aquaculture industry of the Kombumerri Peoples farming mangrove worms, or land transformation through terraces at Wagadagam; identify specific plants or animals and the products they provide
Identify products that can be designed and produced from plants and animals — food products, paper and wood products, fabrics and yarns; trace one product from source to finished item

response_modes.reason: Students need a range of plant-source and animal-source examples before they can generalise the concept that living things are grown and managed for production purposes. A single example (cows for milk) does not build the category. Accumulating examples across food, clothing and shelter contexts builds the breadth needed for the 'explore' command term.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The First Nations aquaculture and land management directions are genuinely rich — they show that growing plants and animals for food includes sophisticated land and water management systems developed over millennia, broadening the concept well beyond a vegetable garden.
success_criteria: Names at least one plant and one animal used as a source for food, clothing or shelter
Identifies at least one product derived from each source
nodes.hinge_reason: Without a populated repertoire of plant and animal sources, Node 2 (how and where they are grown) has no examples to explore — students cannot investigate growing methods for sources they have not yet identified.

nodes.label: How and where plants and animals are grown
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explore how and where plants and animals are grown for food, clothing and shelter in Australia
nodes.minimum_width: Identify where at least one plant or animal is grown in Australia and describe how it is grown or managed for a purpose
nodes.typical_width: Explore how plants and animals are grown in different Australian regions for different purposes — citrus in South Australia, cotton in NSW, timber in Tasmania; describe how tools and equipment are used in growing and harvesting; connect growing methods to the product produced
wider: Compare traditional and contemporary growing methods for the same product — for example hand tools versus GPS-guided tractors for wheat; identify how technology changes what is possible
Consider a range of tools used to grow plants for a purpose — from home garden tools (spade, rake) to large-scale equipment (seed spreader, drone); explain what each tool enables and why it is used

response_modes.reason: Students often have a home-garden mental model for how plants are grown — small, familiar, manual. Encountering growing at different scales (home garden vs cotton farm vs forestry plantation) in different Australian regions builds a more accurate and varied understanding of food and materials production.

success_criteria: Names at least one location in Australia where a plant or animal is grown
Describes how it is grown or managed for its purpose
